lessons.title: Cell differentiation in animals and plants
lessons.text:
## Cell differentiation in animals and plants
LV: GCSE · Foundation
S: Every animal and plant starts as one cell, yet ends up with nerve, muscle, root and leaf cells that each do a different job. Differentiation is how that variety arises, and it is what lets a many-celled body work at all.
O: Explain why differentiation is important for a multicellular organism
O: Compare when animal cells and plant cells differentiate during their lives
O: Describe how a differentiating cell becomes specialised, and state what cell division is mainly used for in adult animals
PRE: Stem cells
REQ: aqa-gcse-biology:4.1.1.4.a @1
REQ: aqa-gcse-biology:4.1.1.4.b @2
REQ: aqa-gcse-biology:4.1.1.4.c @3
T: Differentiation | The process by which an unspecialised cell becomes a specialised cell type, with structures suited to one function
T: Specialised cell | A cell that has differentiated and has the sub-cellular structures it needs to do a particular job
T: Undifferentiated cell | A cell that has not yet specialised, such as a stem cell
T: Stem cell | An undifferentiated cell that can make more cells of its own type and cells that go on to differentiate
T: Meristem | A region near the tips of plant shoots and roots where cells divide and can become any type of plant cell
H: From one cell to many kinds
P: A multicellular organism begins life as a single fertilised egg cell, the **zygote**. The zygote divides again and again. As the new cells are made, they also change into cells with different roles. This change is called **differentiation**: an unspecialised cell becomes a more specialised type of cell, with features that suit one particular job.
P: A cell that has not specialised yet is **undifferentiated**. A **stem cell** is an example: it can make more cells like itself, and it can also make cells that go on to differentiate.
D: bio-stem-cell-potency
H: How a cell becomes specialised
P: While a cell differentiates, it gains new **sub-cellular structures** (the parts inside the cell). Those structures are what allow it to do its job. Once it has them, it is a **specialised cell**.
P: Plants show this clearly. New cells are made near the tip of a shoot. As they get older and end up further from the tip, they grow larger and develop vacuoles, and become differentiated cells.
P: All the body cells of one organism carry the same genetic information, because mitosis copies it exactly into each new cell. Cell types differ because each type uses only some of its genes. Using only the genes it needs saves the cell energy and space.
!: Thinking that differentiated cells have different DNA. Every body cell in an organism carries the same genetic information; what differs is which genes each cell actually uses.
X: Trace one line of differentiation in a human, from the zygote to a blood cell.
> The zygote divides many times to form an embryo made of unspecialised cells.
> Early in development, most of these cells differentiate into the body's many cell types.
> In the adult, only a small number of stem cells remain, in some tissues such as bone marrow.
> Bone marrow stem cells divide, and their daughter cells differentiate into blood cells and immune cells only, not into nerve or muscle cells.
> Each new blood cell gains the structures it needs for its job, so it is now a specialised cell.
H: Animals and plants differ
- **Animals:** most kinds of animal cell differentiate early, while the animal is still developing. After that, few cells can become new types.
- **Adult animals:** cell division is used mostly to mend damaged tissue and to replace cells that wear out. Adult stem cells are few, and each kind makes only related cell types: bone marrow makes blood and immune cells.
- **Plants:** many plant cells can still differentiate for the whole of the plant's life. **Meristem** cells near shoot and root tips divide and can become any type of plant cell at any time.
!: Thinking animals and plants keep differentiating in the same way. Most animal cell types differentiate early, but many plant cells keep the ability for life.
!: Thinking specialised cells in adult animals keep dividing freely. In a mature animal, division is mostly limited to repair and replacement.
K: Differentiation turns unspecialised cells into specialised cells by giving them the sub-cellular structures for one job. Most animal cells do this early in life; many plant cells, especially in meristems, can do it throughout life.
H: Why differentiation matters
P: One cell cannot do every job a large organism needs. Differentiation lets cells share out the work. Different specialised cells, and the tissues and organ systems they build, each carry out a separate job, such as transport, movement, carrying nerve signals, reproduction or photosynthesis.
P: When an exam question asks you to explain why differentiation is important, make the link in steps: cells become specialised, so each type can carry out a particular function, so an organism made of many cell types can carry out all the jobs it needs to stay alive.
K: Differentiation matters because it produces cells with different functions, which together let a multicellular organism carry out many different jobs.
H: Examples to know
P: AQA expects you to know some specialised animal cells (sperm, nerve and muscle cells) and plant cells (root hair, xylem and phloem cells), and to link each cell's structures to its function. Good answers always name a structure and say how it helps the cell do its job.
GAP: The brief does not describe the structures of sperm, nerve, muscle, root hair, xylem and phloem cells, so their structure-to-function links are not taught here.
Q: What is cell differentiation? | The process in which an unspecialised cell becomes a specialised cell type, with structures suited to one job.
Q: When do most animal cells differentiate? | Early, while the animal is still developing.
Q: Where in a plant can cells keep dividing and differentiating throughout life? | In meristems, near the tips of shoots and roots.
Q: What is cell division mainly used for in an adult animal? | Repairing damaged tissue and replacing cells that wear out.
Q: A nerve cell and a muscle cell from one person have the same DNA. Why are they different? | Each cell type uses a different set of its genes.
Q: What does a cell gain as it differentiates? | New sub-cellular structures that let it carry out its particular function.
M1@3: What happens to a cell as it differentiates? | It gains sub-cellular structures suited to a particular job | It loses the genes it will not need in its new job | It returns to being an unspecialised stem cell again | It splits into two cells with different genetic information | Differentiation gives a cell the structures it needs for one function; its genetic information stays the same as in other body cells.
M1@2: Where in a plant are there cells that divide and can become any type of plant cell? | Meristems near the shoot and root tips | Cells in the middle layer of a leaf | Xylem cells running up through the stem | Root hair cells on the outside of a root | Meristems keep dividing throughout the plant's life, and their cells can differentiate into any plant cell type.
M2@2: Which statement correctly compares differentiation in plants and animals? | Many plant cells keep the ability to differentiate for life; most animal cells differentiate early | Most plant cells differentiate early; many animal cells keep the ability to differentiate for life | Plant and animal cells both keep the same ability to differentiate all through their lives | Plant and animal cells all finish differentiating before the animal is born or the seed grows | Most animal cell types differentiate early in development, while many plant cells, such as those in meristems, can differentiate at any time.
M2@3: In an adult human, what is cell division mainly used for? | Repairing damaged tissue and replacing worn-out cells | Producing new types of cell the body never had before | Making every organ keep growing larger throughout life | Turning muscle cells into nerve cells whenever needed | In mature animals most cells have already differentiated, so division is mostly limited to repair and replacement.
M2@3: Stem cells from an adult's bone marrow are grown in a laboratory. Which cells can they form? | Blood cells and immune cells | Nerve cells and muscle cells | Any cell type the body needs | Skin cells and liver cells | Adult stem cells are few and form only related cell types; bone marrow stem cells give rise to blood and immune cells.
M3@1: A student says differentiation is important because it makes cells divide faster. Which answer best explains its real importance? | It makes cells with different functions, so a many-celled organism can carry out many different jobs | It makes many identical copies of the zygote, so that the organism can grow much larger quickly | It changes the DNA in each cell, so that different cells can follow different sets of instructions | It keeps every cell unspecialised, so that any cell can take over from any other cell that is damaged | Specialised cells each carry out a particular function, and together their tissues and organ systems let the organism do everything it needs.
SA3@1,2,3: Explain why differentiation is important to a multicellular organism, and explain why a plant can go on forming new types of cell throughout its life when an adult animal mostly cannot. | As cells differentiate they gain sub-cellular structures that suit them to one function, so they become specialised. Different specialised cells, and the tissues and organ systems they form, carry out separate jobs such as transport, movement and reproduction, so the organism can do everything it needs. In plants, many cells keep the ability to differentiate for life, and meristem cells near shoot and root tips can become any plant cell type at any time. Most animal cells differentiate early, so in an adult animal division is mainly for repair and replacement, and adult stem cells form only related cell types. | Cells gain structures and become specialised ; Links specialisation to carrying out functions in the organism ; Plant cells keep the ability to differentiate for life ; Meristems at shoot and root tips ; Most animal cells differentiate early ; Adult animal division mainly for repair and replacement
SUM: Differentiation is the process by which an unspecialised cell becomes a specialised cell suited to one job.
SUM: As a cell differentiates it gains the sub-cellular structures it needs to carry out its function.
SUM: Most animal cells differentiate early in development, but many plant cells, especially in meristems, can differentiate throughout life.
SUM: In adult animals, cell division is mainly used to repair tissue and replace cells.
SUM: Differentiation is important because specialised cells with different functions let a multicellular organism carry out many jobs.
